opus-5.5.text:
I think of it as a relationship between a teacher and a student, or maybe more precisely, between a very large brain in the cloud and a very efficient, very fast brain in the car.

In the cloud, you have the foundation model: enormous parameters, trained on massive amounts of data, including real driving data, simulation data, and increasingly world-model-generated data. That model has very broad knowledge. It understands long-tail scenarios, it can reason about rare events, and it can generate new scenarios to test against. But you can't put that model in the vehicle. The latency, the compute, the power budget, the cost, none of it works. A car has maybe a few hundred to a thousand TOPS, and it has to make decisions in tens of milliseconds.

So the vehicle model is essentially a distilled version. The cloud model teaches it through distillation, through data labeling, through generating training data, through reinforcement learning in simulated environments. The vehicle model is smaller, specialized, and optimized for real-time perception, prediction, and planning, increasingly in an end-to-end fashion.

Then there's the loop going the other way. The fleet on the road is a giant sensor network. When a car encounters a corner case, a disengagement, or something the onboard model is uncertain about, that data flows back to the cloud. The cloud model analyzes it, retrains, generates variations in simulation, and pushes an updated model back to the vehicle. That's the data flywheel, and whoever runs that flywheel fastest and most efficiently has the advantage.

There's also a third piece people sometimes overlook: the roadside and the infrastructure. At Tsinghua's AIR, we've worked a lot on vehicle-infrastructure cooperation. I call it "smart car plus smart road." The road can provide beyond-line-of-sight information, and the cloud can coordinate at a city level. So in my view the full architecture is cloud, road, and vehicle, three layers working together.

One more point. Safety-critical decisions must stay onboard. You can't depend on the network for braking. The cloud is for learning, improving, and coordinating, not for real-time control. That separation is essential.

So in short: a big model in the cloud that is broad and deep, a small model in the car that is fast and reliable, continuous distillation and feedback between them, with the road as an additional layer of intelligence. I believe that's how we'll get to L4 at scale.

r001.rationale: The response compares the cloud and vehicle models to a teacher and student and to large and efficient brains. It does not liken the architecture to an operating-system ecosystem spanning the cloud and a phone.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think of it as a two-layer system, and it's actually not that different from how Microsoft and Baidu approached cloud computing years ago. You have a large foundation model in the cloud, and you have a much smaller, highly optimized model running on the vehicle itself. They do different things, and the architecture is about how they talk to each other.

The cloud model is big. It's trained on all the data that comes back from the fleet, millions of kilometers, every corner case, every near miss. It has essentially unlimited compute and unlimited time. So it can do things like world modeling, long-horizon reasoning, generating synthetic scenarios, and it can continuously improve. Think of it as the teacher.

The vehicle model has to make decisions in tens of milliseconds, on a chip with maybe a few hundred TOPS and a strict power budget. It can't afford to be large. So what we do is distill the knowledge from the cloud model into the on-board model. The cloud model acts as the teacher, the vehicle model is the student. You compress, quantize, prune, and you end up with something that runs in real time but carries most of the intelligence of the big model.

Then there's the data loop going the other direction. The vehicle encounters situations the small model is uncertain about, those get flagged, uploaded, labeled, and they go back into training the cloud model. That closed loop is really the heart of the whole thing. The cloud learns from the fleet, the fleet gets smarter from the cloud. Each cycle the gap between them narrows a little.

One thing I'd emphasize is that latency and safety dictate the boundary. Anything safety-critical, perception, planning, control, must run locally. You cannot depend on a network connection to brake. The cloud handles what's non-real-time: training, simulation, high-definition map updates, fleet-level learning. So the split isn't arbitrary, it's determined by physics and by what happens when the connection drops.

And I think going forward, with end-to-end models and the multimodal foundation models we're seeing now, the line blurs a bit. The on-board model starts to look more like a smaller version of a general world model rather than a stack of separate modules. But the basic architecture, big model in the cloud, small model in the car, a data flywheel connecting them, I think that stays.

r001.rationale: The response describes a cloud model paired with an onboard vehicle model, but it does not liken that architecture to an operating-system ecosystem spanning the cloud and a phone.

astra-6.text:
I think of it as a cloud–vehicle collaboration, with different responsibilities on each side. In the cloud, you can have a much larger model, with the computing resources to learn from fleet data, generate scenarios, run simulations, and train better driving models. In the vehicle, you need a model that can perceive, predict, and act in real time, within very strict limits on latency, power, and computing capacity.

The connection is a continuous learning loop. The vehicle encounters situations that help us identify gaps; those cases inform training and validation in the cloud; and validated improvements are then deployed back to the vehicle. Distillation is one way to transfer capabilities from the larger cloud model into a smaller onboard model.

But the vehicle must be able to drive safely without a network connection. The cloud supports learning and improvement; the onboard system has responsibility for the immediate driving decisions. So the architecture combines the scale of cloud intelligence with the responsiveness and independence of intelligence in the vehicle.

r001.rationale: The response describes cloud and onboard vehicle models as a collaboration, but it does not compare the architecture to an operating-system ecosystem spanning the cloud and a phone.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of it as a cloud–vehicle architecture with a continuous learning loop. In the cloud, you have a much larger model, with more computing power, that can learn from driving data, run simulations, and help train and evaluate the models deployed in vehicles. In the car, you need a model that can perceive, reason, and act in real time, within very strict limits on latency, power, and computing resources.

The key is that the vehicle must be able to drive safely on its own. You cannot depend on a cloud connection for a braking decision. The cloud helps improve the vehicle’s intelligence over time, while the vehicle handles the immediate driving task. Difficult situations encountered on the road can feed back into training and simulation, and validated improvements can then be deployed to the fleet. So these are complementary models, connected through learning, rather than a cloud model remotely driving the car.

r001.rationale: The response describes complementary cloud and in-vehicle models connected through learning, but does not liken the architecture to an operating-system ecosystem spanning the cloud and a phone.
